questions.question: What’s our most popular payment method?
questions.sql:
SELECT payment_type,
       count(*) AS payments,
       count(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders,
       round(100.0 * count(*) / sum(count(*)) OVER (), 2) AS pct_of_payments
FROM order_payments
GROUP BY payment_type
ORDER BY payments DESC
LIMIT 1
questions.note: "Most popular" is ranked by the number of payment records for each method. The query also shows how many distinct orders used that method.

questions.question: What’s the average review score across all orders?
questions.sql:
WITH order_scores AS (
  SELECT order_id, avg(review_score) AS order_score
  FROM order_reviews
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT round(avg(order_score), 2) AS avg_review_score,
       count(*) AS reviewed_orders
FROM order_scores
questions.note: Each order counts once, using the average of its reviews if it has several, and orders with no review are left out.

       round(sum(oi.price), 2) AS revenue

ORDER BY revenue DESC

       round(avg(extract(epoch FROM o.order_delivered_customer_date - o.order_purchase_timestamp) / 86400)::numeric, 2) AS avg_delivery_days

questions.question: Do customers who pay in more installments spend more per order?
questions.sql:
WITH per_order AS (
  SELECT order_id,
         max(payment_installments) AS installments,
         sum(payment_value) AS order_spend
  FROM order_payments
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT installments,
       count(*) AS orders,
       round(avg(order_spend), 2) AS avg_spend_per_order,
       round(percentile_cont(0.5) WITHIN GROUP (ORDER BY order_spend)::numeric, 2) AS median_spend_per_order
FROM per_order
GROUP BY installments
ORDER BY installments
questions.note: Spend per order is the sum of all payments on the order. Each order is placed by its largest installment count across its payment methods. All order statuses are included, because this compares average payments rather than sales.

questions.question: How did monthly revenue trend in 2018 compared to the same months in 2017?
questions.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT extract(year FROM o.order_purchase_timestamp)::int AS yr,
         extract(month FROM o.order_purchase_timestamp)::int AS mon,
         sum(p.payment_value) AS revenue
  FROM order_payments p
  JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = p.order_id
  WHERE o.order_status NOT IN ('canceled', 'unavailable')
    AND o.order_purchase_timestamp >= '2017-01-01'
    AND o.order_purchase_timestamp < '2019-01-01'
    AND extract(month FROM o.order_purchase_timestamp) <= 8
  GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT mon AS month,
       round(sum(revenue) FILTER (WHERE yr = 2017), 2) AS revenue_2017,
       round(sum(revenue) FILTER (WHERE yr = 2018), 2) AS revenue_2018,
       round(100.0 * (sum(revenue) FILTER (WHERE yr = 2018) - sum(revenue) FILTER (WHERE yr = 2017))
             / nullif(sum(revenue) FILTER (WHERE yr = 2017), 0), 2) AS yoy_growth_pct
FROM monthly
GROUP BY mon
ORDER BY mon
questions.note: The comparison covers January to August only, because the 2018 data effectively ends in August: September 2018 has 16 orders and October 2018 has 4.

questions.question: Are late deliveries hurting our review scores? Compare on-time vs. late orders.

WITH delivered AS (
  SELECT o.order_id,
         CASE WHEN o.order_delivered_customer_date > o.order_estimated_delivery_date

  FROM orders o
  WHERE o.order_status = 'delivered'
    AND o.order_delivered_customer_date IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT d.delivery_group,
       count(DISTINCT d.order_id) AS reviewed_orders,
       count(*) AS review_rows,
       round(avg(r.review_score), 2) AS avg_score,
       round(100.0 * avg(CASE WHEN r.review_score <= 2 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS pct_low_scores,
       round(100.0 * avg(CASE WHEN r.review_score = 5 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END), 2) AS pct_five_star
FROM delivered d
JOIN order_reviews r ON r.order_id = d.order_id
GROUP BY d.delivery_group
ORDER BY d.delivery_group
questions.note: This uses delivered orders that have a delivery date, counts an order as late when it arrived after the estimated date, and averages the review rows for those orders.

questions.question: For each of the top 3 categories by revenue, which month in 2018 was their best?
questions.sql:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT coalesce(p.product_category_name_english, 'unknown') AS category,
         date_trunc('month', o.order_purchase_timestamp)::date AS month,
         sum(oi.price) AS revenue
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  JOIN products p ON p.product_id = oi.product_id
  WHERE o.order_status NOT IN ('canceled', 'unavailable')
    AND o.order_purchase_timestamp >= '2018-01-01' AND o.order_purchase_timestamp < '2019-01-01'
  GROUP BY 1, 2
),
top_cats AS (
  SELECT category, sum(revenue) AS total_revenue
  FROM monthly
  GROUP BY category
  ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
  LIMIT 3
),
ranked AS (
  SELECT m.category, m.month, m.revenue, t.total_revenue,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY m.category ORDER BY m.revenue DESC) AS rn
  FROM monthly m
  JOIN top_cats t ON t.category = m.category
)
SELECT category,
       round(total_revenue, 2) AS revenue_2018,
       month AS best_month,
       round(revenue, 2) AS best_month_revenue
FROM ranked
WHERE rn = 1
ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
questions.note: This ranks the top 3 categories by their 2018 item revenue (SUM of price, excluding canceled and unavailable orders). Note that 2018 data effectively ends in August, so September to December are nearly or entirely empty.

questions.question: Which sellers had sales increase every quarter in 2018?
questions.sql:
WITH seller_q AS (
  SELECT oi.seller_id,
         sum(oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.order_purchase_timestamp >= '2018-01-01' AND o.order_purchase_timestamp < '2018-04-01') AS q1,
         sum(oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.order_purchase_timestamp >= '2018-04-01' AND o.order_purchase_timestamp < '2018-07-01') AS q2,
         sum(oi.price) FILTER (WHERE o.order_purchase_timestamp >= '2018-07-01' AND o.order_purchase_timestamp < '2018-10-01') AS q3
  FROM order_items oi
  JOIN orders o ON o.order_id = oi.order_id
  WHERE o.order_status NOT IN ('canceled', 'unavailable')
    AND o.order_purchase_timestamp >= '2018-01-01' AND o.order_purchase_timestamp < '2018-10-01'
  GROUP BY oi.seller_id
)
SELECT q.seller_id,
       s.seller_state AS state,
       round(q.q1, 2) AS q1_sales,
       round(q.q2, 2) AS q2_sales,
       round(q.q3, 2) AS q3_sales
FROM seller_q q
JOIN sellers s ON s.seller_id = q.seller_id
WHERE q.q1 > 0 AND q.q2 > q.q1 AND q.q3 > q.q2
ORDER BY q3_sales DESC
questions.note: Sales here means the sum of item prices, excluding freight and canceled or unavailable orders, and a seller must have sales in each of Q1–Q3 2018 with each quarter strictly higher than the one before. 2018 data effectively ends in August, so Q3 covers only July and August and Q4 cannot be assessed.

questions.question: What’s the average time between a repeat customer’s first and second order?
questions.sql:
WITH ordered AS (
  SELECT c.customer_unique_id, o.order_purchase_timestamp,
         row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY c.customer_unique_id ORDER BY o.order_purchase_timestamp) AS n
  FROM orders o
  JOIN customers c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
), pairs AS (
  SELECT customer_unique_id,
         max(order_purchase_timestamp) FILTER (WHERE n = 2)
           - max(order_purchase_timestamp) FILTER (WHERE n = 1) AS gap
  FROM ordered
  WHERE n <= 2
  GROUP BY customer_unique_id
  HAVING count(*) = 2
)
SELECT round(avg(extract(epoch FROM gap) / 86400)::numeric, 2) AS avg_days_between
FROM pairs
questions.note: This treats a repeat customer as a unique person (`customer_unique_id`) with at least two orders of any status, and reports the gap between their first two purchases in days.
